title: CVE-2026-125294 - Nexter Blocks Pro <= 5.0.10 - Unauthenticated Privilege Escalation to Unicode Collation Confusion in 'tpgb_acf_key' Parameter
text:
9.8

CRITICAL
CVSS 3.1

CVE-2026-125294
Nexter Blocks Pro <= 5.0.10 - Unauthenticated Privilege Escalation to Unicode Collation Confusion in 'tpgb_acf_key' Parameter

The Nexter Blocks Pro plugin for WordPress is vulnerable to Privilege Escalation in all versions up to, and including, 5.0.10 via the `tpgb_ajax_register_user()` function. This is due to a byte-level denylist on the `tpgb_acf_key[]` and `tpgb_acf[]` parameters that fails to block Unicode look-alike characters — such as U+1E87 and U+00E7 in a key like `ẇp_çapabilities` — whose UTF-8 byte sequences do not match any ASCII-based pattern check, while the database's default accent-insensitive collation (`utf8mb4_unicode_ci` / `utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci`) treats the decorated key as equivalent to the canonical `wp_capabilities` row, causing `update_user_meta()` to overwrite the newly registered user's role with `administrator`. This makes it possible for unauthenticated attackers to register a new account bearing the full Administrator role, gaining complete control over the WordPress site including the ability to install plugins, modify files, and execute arbitrary code. The nonce required by the handler is publicly emitted on any page containing the tp-login-register block, making the full exploit chain — nonce retrieval, a single crafted registration POST, and the plugin's own `autologin` flow — trivially reachable on any default install where user registration is enabled. Successful exploitation causes the attacker's own account to receive the complete Administrator role.

text:

HIGH
CVSS 4.0

CVE-2026-134461
Web-Token jwt-framework before 3.4.10 DoS via Unbounded PBES2 p2c Iteration Count

Web-Token jwt-framework and jwt-library before 3.4.10, 4.0.0 before 4.0.7, and 4.1.0 before 4.1.7 contain an uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability in PBES2AESKW::unwrapKey(), which passes the attacker-controlled p2c JWE header value to hash_pbkdf2() without an upper bound. Unauthenticated attackers can send a JWE using a PBES2-HS*+A*KW algorithm with a huge p2c iteration count to force lengthy PBKDF2 computations and exhaust server CPU.

title: CVE-2026-134459 - web-token jwt-framework before 3.4.10 RSA1_5 Bleichenbacher Padding Oracle
text:
8.2

HIGH
CVSS 4.0

CVE-2026-134459
web-token jwt-framework before 3.4.10 RSA1_5 Bleichenbacher Padding Oracle

web-token jwt-framework and jwt-library before 3.4.10, 4.0.x before 4.0.7, and 4.1.x before 4.1.7 contain a padding oracle in RSACrypt::decryptWithRSA15() because RSA1_5 decryption lacks implicit rejection, so invalid padding, wrong CEK length, and valid padding take measurably different time. Remote attackers can submit adaptively crafted JWE encrypted_key values and measure these timing differences to recover the wrapped content encryption key.

title: CVE-2026-134458 - web-token jwt-framework before 3.4.12 ECDH-ES Weak Key Derivation via ConcatKDF
text:
8.2

HIGH
CVSS 4.0

CVE-2026-134458
web-token jwt-framework before 3.4.12 ECDH-ES Weak Key Derivation via ConcatKDF

web-token jwt-framework and jwt-library before 3.4.12, 4.0.x before 4.0.8, 4.1.x before 4.1.10, and 4.2.x before 4.2.4, and jwt-encryption-algorithm-ecdh-es through 3.2.10, have a ConcatKDF::generate() that performs a single SHA-256 round, deriving at most 32 bytes for ECDH-ES and ECDH-SS direct key agreement. Anyone holding a JWE using A256CBC-HS512 can decrypt it under an all-zero AES key, while A192CBC-HS384 content keys have only 64-bit strength.

Suspected China-linked hackers used autonomous AI agents to find a previously unknown flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source medical imaging server, and gain root access to a university server, Amazon Threat Intelligence said this week.

The flaw allows an attacker with no account to write files outside the server's storage folder, and it affects MONAI Label 0.8.5 and earlier in the default setup, which runs with no login enabled.

The maintainers have merged a fix in the source code, but there is still no fixed version to install.

MONAI Label is a server that research teams use to label medical scans and train imaging models; it is a separate program from the broader MONAI framework.

The weakness is a path-traversal flaw in the parts of the server that store uploaded images and labels. A file identifier supplied by the caller is appended to the storage folder and written to disk without checking that the result remains within that folder.

The server writes with the privileges of the account it runs under, so an attacker cannot write anywhere on the machine, but a writable code or settings location can open a path to running code. Authentication is off by default, so any client that can reach the server over the network can set off the write. Versions 0.8.5 and earlier are affected.

Amazon reconstructed the intrusion after finding the operator's own Cairn control panel sitting on the internet without a password. Cairn is an open-source framework that runs AI agents as automated penetration testers, and the exposed panel revealed the agents' task settings, prompts, and run history.

Over about 48 hours in September, the agents mapped the application's interface and reached the point of writing files to the server in roughly 11 minutes, the company said in its incident report.

The agents worked with little step-by-step direction. The operator set the goal of getting shell access and chose the targets, and the agents selected the methods themselves, according to the company.

Investigators tie the campaign to a China-linked actor with moderate confidence, pointing to Simplified Chinese prompts, China Standard Time settings, and targets likely of interest to China. They did not connect the work to a named group or establish that a government was behind it.

A root shell came later, and not within those 11 minutes. In a separate session, the agents used the same flaw to plant a file that Python runs automatically at startup. They then triggered a training feature that started a new Python process, which loaded that file and connected back to the attacker as root.

That root access was on one university server, and whether another MONAI Label system would give the same result depends on how it is run and what its service account can do.

In a later session, the operator handed the agents a tunnel into a second university network running the same software. Amazon believes the network was broken into in the same way but has not confirmed the second compromise.

The maintainers confirmed the flaw and merged the source fix on October 19, which forces uploads to resolve inside the approved folders and rejects empty names or names that begin with a dot.

Their security advisory, published earlier this week, still lists no patched version and says the correction will arrive in a future release. The newest release listing remains 0.8.5, which dates to 2024. A merged fix in source code is not the same as a package you can install.

title: CTO of ‘RansomwareHelp’ Indicted for Wire Fraud
text:
The chief technology officer and co-founder of ransomwarehelp.com, a six year old Florida business that claimed to use “advanced cryptographic tools” to restore data locked by ransomware, has been charged with wire fraud after an FBI sting operation found the company was simply paying the attackers for a decryption key and charging victims a markup for work that was never performed.
A portion of the now-defunct website ransomwarehelp.com.
The website RansomwareHelp urged victims “Do not pay the ransom!,” claiming its advanced cryptographic tools could restore 100 percent of data, servers, and systems to their original format, and that there was no need to give in to extortion demands.
“Our cryptography experts use proprietary tools and algorithms to achieve 100% data recovery, all backed by a success rate of over 99%,” the website enthused, claiming the company had over 28 years of experience and a team of 80 experts in cryptography, cybersecurity, forensic analysis and reverse engineering. “We never promote, intermediate or pay ransom to threat actors on behalf of our clients.”
But according to an indictment (PDF) returned this week in Rhode Island, the company’s co-founder — 52-year-old Juan Ricardo Palacio Escobar of Miami and Medellin, Colombia — routinely paid ransomware groups for a decryption key to unlock victim data, and then charged those victims well above what he’d secretly paid the threat actors [Palacio’s indictment was reported earlier this week by 404 Media, but for some reason that story did not name the defendant’s company].
The indictment says the FBI set up a sting operation in which the feds were posing both as a ransomware victim company and as a fictitious ransomware group. Pretending to be victims of a cyberattack, investigators contacted RansomwareHelp and supplied the company with a copy of a phony ransomware note, saying they did not wish to pay a ransom. RansomwareHelp replied by reiterating its policy against negotiating with or making ransom payments to threat actors.
The government said Palacio soon after contacted the fake ransomware group run by the FBI and requested the lowest possible price for the decryptor. FBI investigators responded with a price of .2 bitcoin, or around $13,000 at the time. Less than 48 hours later, Palacio allegedly told agents acting as the victim company that the diagnostic assessment was successful and that the cost of decrypting the files would be $13,260.
The following day, the government alleges, Palacio messaged the fictitious ransomware group operated by the feds and asked to reduce the ransom demand to $4,000 for the purchase of a decryption tool. The indictment states that the agreed upon price was around $6,000 in bitcoin, and that Palacio charged the FBI’s fake victim firm $16,010, including an initial $2,750 diagnostic fee and the full fee of $13,260.
Paul Ihme is co-founder of the security firm Soteria. Ihme told KrebsOnSecurity that in 2024 he heard from a small accounting firm that had paid RansomwareHelp a diagnostic fee to help recover from a Lockbit ransomware infection that had locked all of their company and client data.
Ihme said RansomwareHelp sent a proposal to the victim with a recovery price of $438,880, which it claimed included “professional configuration of forensic servers,” “expert engineering hours of programming to configure decryption algorithms,” and “eight (6-hour processing cycles) related to the decryption process.”
A portion of the proposal that RansomwareHelp sent to a victim accounting firm in March 2024. Click to enlarge.
The proposal stated that the recovery process involved reverse engineering the ransomware encryption using “510 preconfigured forensic servers of the maximum quantitative capacity located in different parts of the world.”
“Our programmers will inject randomly the encryption codes extracted during the forensic and cryptographic analysis using brute force processes,” the proposal claimed.

Cyberattack on Austrian Foreign Ministry Exposes Diplomatic Staff Data

Pierluigi Paganini
November 21, 2026

Austrian Foreign Ministry Hacked, Staff Contact Details Accessed

Hackers accessed Austrian Foreign Ministry records containing staff contact details, including employees at diplomatic missions abroad.

Austrian Foreign Ministry confirmed a cyberattack against its website that exposed staff contact information, including details of employees working at diplomatic missions abroad. The security breach occurred between November 12 and 13, during a global Microsoft outage, and raises questions about the security of government websites and the risks associated with services managed by external providers.

According to the ministry, attackers gained unauthorized access to a website operated by an external service provider. The intrusion was detected on November 13, and authorities said they stopped it immediately.

“”Between November 12 and 13, the foreign ministry’s website, which is operated by an external service provider, was accessed in an unauthorized ​manner,” the ministry said in a statement, adding that it happened ​during a global Microsoft outage.” Reuters reports.

The ministry confirmed that the hack was detected on November 13 ⁠and government staff stopped it immediately.

An investigation by a team of cybersecurity experts found that the intruders had viewed records containing the names and professional contact details of ministry employees. The information covered both staff at the ministry’s headquarters in Vienna and personnel working at Austrian diplomatic missions abroad.

“An investigation by a team of experts ​found that during the unauthorized access, data records were viewed that listed ​the names and work contact details of employees at ministry headquarters as well as at diplomatic missions abroad,” the ministry added.

The Austrian authorities have not disclosed how many records were accessed, whether the attackers copied the information, or how they managed to enter the website. They have also not identified the vulnerability or attack technique used.

The ministry stressed that the incident did not affect citizens’ personal information. According to Austrian public broadcaster ORF, the authorities reported the incident to the Federal Office for Cyber Security and the Data Protection Authority, while also launching additional technical security checks.

“The Foreign Ministry emphasized that it was taking the incident “very seriously.” The integrity of the infrastructure was of the highest priority. The systems were subject to strict security regulations and continuous monitoring, it stated. The incident had also prompted additional technical security checks.” states ORF. “The Foreign Ministry has been repeatedly targeted by cyberattacks. At the beginning of 2020, there was a serious cyberattack that lasted until February. In April 2022, there were cyberattacks involving phishing emails.”

The timing of the incident is also noteworthy. The ministry said the intrusion coincided with a global Microsoft service outage, but it hasn’t established any connection between the two events. A major service disruption can complicate incident response and monitoring, but the available information doesn’t show that attackers exploited the outage to gain access.

Attribution remains another unanswered question. The ministry hasn’t named any suspected country or threat group, and there’s no evidence linking this particular intrusion to a state-sponsored operation.

However, the incident comes against a difficult diplomatic background. Austria has maintained military neutrality but has politically supported Ukraine since Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. text:

CVE-2026-84448 is an out-of-bounds read (CWE-125) in libheif, a widely used HEIF and AVIF image decoder/encoder library, affecting all versions prior to 1.23.2. The flaw resides in the writer API path — specifically heif_region_item_add_region_inline_mask_data() in libheif/api/libheif/heif_regions.cc — which accepts an attacker- or caller-supplied mask_data_len without validating it against the byte count implied by the region's width and height. When a later heif_region_get_mask_image() call derives its read length from the region geometry, an undersized buffer causes heif_region_get_inline_mask_image() to read and copy adjacent heap bytes into the returned monochrome mask image, disclosing heap memory or crashing the host application.
The CVSS base score is 4.0 (Medium), reflecting a local attack vector, high attack complexity, no privileges required, and low confidentiality and availability impact. Critically, the file-parsing path is not vulnerable — it validates the canonical mask size — so exploitation requires an application that constructs region metadata programmatically through the writer API rather than by parsing an untrusted file. There is no public proof-of-concept, no Nuclei template, no exploit code, and the CVE is not listed in CISA KEV.

Vulnerability Mechanism
The defect is an information-disclosure and availability issue rooted in a heap buffer over-read. In libheif's region API, inline mask data is stored alongside region geometry (width and height). The byte count required to fully describe a monochrome mask is a deterministic function of those two dimensions — a caller storing a mask must supply exactly that many bytes.
CVE-2026-84448 arises because heif_region_item_add_region_inline_mask_data() in libheif/api/libheif/heif_regions.cc accepts the caller-supplied length parameter mask_data_len without verifying that it equals the byte count required by the accompanying width and height. The stored buffer is therefore permitted to be smaller than the geometry implies.
The inconsistency only manifests on retrieval. A subsequent heif_region_get_mask_image() call derives the amount of data to read from the region geometry rather than from the stored buffer length. It delegates to heif_region_get_inline_mask_image(), which then reads beyond the end of the undersized heap allocation and copies the adjacent bytes into the returned monochrome mask image.

Confidentiality (C:L) — heap contents adjacent to the mask buffer are copied into the returned mask image. An application that subsequently writes, transmits, or displays that image can leak those bytes.
Availability (A:L) — if the over-read crosses a heap allocation boundary into an unmapped page, the process can crash, taking down the host application.

Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV–style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.
Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.
Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.
The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.
“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”

So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.
1. Start with a presumption of innocence–or negligence
The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.
As the head of Internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One’s default position should be that it isn’t a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”
Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” says João Tomé, the Internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”
2. Look at status updates from organizations that might be involved
In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a big cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services, for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.

Threat Actor Profile
PixelLeaks is a low-profile ransomware and data-extortion brand with no established public track record that Yazoul Security can currently corroborate. The group’s total known victim count is unknown, and there is no publicly available research, tooling documentation, or prior campaign analysis attributed to this name.
The actor’s known tools and tactics are, at present, undocumented. The listing’s language - emphasizing “verified” records and a short four-day deadline - is consistent with pressure tactics common across leak sites, but it does not by itself establish credibility. Groups with thin or absent histories frequently borrow terminology and formatting from more established operations, and some are suspected of rebranding or operating as splinter personas. # The NCIC Was Breached. The Access Logs Are a Mess.

The wire says everything is falling apart this afternoon, and someone breached the National Crime Information Center database, which acts as the central nervous system for American law enforcement. People are calling it a catastrophic failure of national security. The loud end of the internet claims some sophisticated adversary got into the FBI's core infrastructure. Now the private details of millions of citizens and criminals are apparently up for sale to the highest bidder; is the state actually this vulnerable? That is how it's being framed.

It is a tidy story. It also ignores how the NCIC actually works.

If you have ever spent time reviewing an audit trail or a disclosure filing, you know that "the database was hacked" is rarely a statement of technical fact and usually a shorthand for "someone had credentials they shouldn't have." The NCIC is not a single, monolithic vault guarded by a few elite engineers in Washington. It is a federation. Thousands of local, state, and tribal agencies plug into it. When the news reports that the FBI was hacked, they are often describing an event where an attacker used compromised credentials from a peripheral endpoint to query the central system.

The breach isn't necessarily a failure of the FBI's perimeter; it is a failure of identity management across a sprawling, fragmented network of thousands of disparate users. If a police department in a small town fails to rotate its passwords or leaves an API key in a public GitHub repo, the attacker doesn't have to "break into" the FBI. They simply walk through the front door using a valid key.

We have seen 538 data breach stories this week. Forty-one of those arrived today alone. In that context, the NCIC incident isn't a unique architectural failure; it is just the most prestigious one on the list. It follows the same pattern as the SBC Medical Group leak that exposed 1.6 million records earlier this week: too many people had access to too much data for too long without a proper audit of who was actually using it.

From a regulatory perspective, this is where things get truly dull and disappointing. In Brussels, a breach of this magnitude in a private firm would trigger a frantic scramble to satisfy GDPR's 72-hour notification window, followed by a fine that might actually make a board member sweat. But when the state breaches itself, there is no independent regulator to issue a penalty. There are only internal reviews and congressional hearings where officials use phrases like "sophisticated actors" to avoid admitting that someone forgot to enable multi-factor authentication on a legacy portal.

The machinery of government regulation is slow because it's designed to be an exercise in paperwork, not a mechanism for correction. The FBI will conduct an investigation, a report will be filed in triplicate, and some budget line item for "modernisation" will be increased by a few million dollars. Nothing actually changes in the workflow because the people writing the rules are the ones who failed to follow them.

The second-order effect here is the real tragedy, and it's one that hasn't made the headlines yet. The NCIC contains sensitive PII on law enforcement officers—home addresses, phone numbers, and family details. While the world worries about "national security" in the abstract, there are now thousands of local cops who may have their home addresses sitting in a leak site. Those officers aren't protected by federal firewalls; they live in suburbs and rural towns. They are the ones currently exposed two steps downstream from the initial breach.

On November 20, 2026, two significant data breaches came to light, resulting in the public exposure of over 4.3 million unique user records on a hacking forum. The first breach targeted Too Lost, a music distribution service for independent artists, exposing the data of over 724,000 users, including extremely sensitive personal identifiable information (PII) like driver's licenses and government IDs. The second, larger breach hit Careers360, an Indian education and career guidance platform, leaking 3.6 million unique email addresses along with names, academic records, and other sensitive personal details. These incidents highlight the ongoing threat of large-scale data theft from web platforms and the significant risk posed to individuals whose data is exposed.
Threat Overview
Too Lost Data Breach

Records Exposed: 724,323 users.
Date of Breach: Early November 2026.
Exposed Data: The breach is particularly severe due to the nature of the data, which includes unique email addresses, names, dates of birth, IP addresses, and, in some cases, highly sensitive PII such as driver's licenses and other government-issued IDs. This type of data is a goldmine for identity thieves.

Careers360 Data Breach

Records Exposed: 22 million total records, containing 3.6 million unique email addresses.
Date of Breach: Allegedly November 14, 2026.
Exposed Data: The leaked dataset contains students' names, phone numbers, genders, academic records, and, notably, caste categories. The inclusion of caste information is highly sensitive within the Indian context and could be used for discrimination or targeted social engineering.

In both cases, the data was stolen from the companies and subsequently published on a public hacking forum, making it widely available to other malicious actors.
Technical Analysis
The most likely attack vectors for breaches of this nature are vulnerabilities in the web applications themselves or their underlying infrastructure.

T1190 - Exploit Public-Facing Application: A common cause is a vulnerability like SQL Injection (SQLi), which allows an attacker to directly query and exfiltrate data from the backend database.
T1566 - Phishing: An attacker could have phished an employee with administrative access to the company's database or application backend.
Misconfigured Cloud Storage: Publicly exposed cloud storage buckets (e.g., Amazon S3) containing database backups or user data are another frequent source of large-scale data leaks.

The publication of the data on a hacking forum indicates the motive was likely reputational damage or to provide data for the broader cybercrime community, rather than direct extortion of the companies.
Impact Assessment
The individuals affected by these breaches face a significant and long-term risk of harm. For Too Lost users, the presence of government ID information creates a direct path to identity theft and financial fraud. Attackers can use this data to open new lines of credit, file fraudulent tax returns, or impersonate victims. For Careers360 users, the combination of academic records, contact information, and caste data can be used for highly targeted phishing scams, blackmail, or social discrimination. Both user bases are now prime targets for follow-on attacks.

On November 21, 2026, Ochsner Health, a major non-profit healthcare provider based in Louisiana, confirmed it was the victim of a data breach. The incident reportedly stemmed from a compromise involving its Microsoft-based systems. While specific details about the attack vector and the scope of exposed data are not yet public, the confirmation has triggered significant concern due to the large volume of sensitive patient data, including Protected Health Information (PHI) under HIPAA, that Ochsner Health manages. The organization has activated its incident response plan and is working to investigate the breach and notify affected parties.
Threat Overview
Details regarding the breach are currently limited. The statement from Ochsner Health points to a compromise "of its systems that utilize Microsoft infrastructure." This broad description could encompass a wide range of scenarios, including but not limited to:

A phishing attack leading to the compromise of a Microsoft 365 account with privileged access.
Exploitation of a vulnerability in an on-premise Microsoft product, such as Exchange Server or SharePoint.
A misconfiguration in its Microsoft Azure cloud environment.
A compromise at a third-party vendor that had access to Ochsner's Microsoft environment.

Given the target is a large healthcare organization, the likely motive is data theft for the purpose of extortion (ransomware) or for sale on dark web forums.
Technical Analysis
Without a specific vector, we must consider common TTPs used against large enterprises running Microsoft environments:

Initial Access: Spearphishing campaigns (T1566.002 - Spearphishing Link) are a primary vector for stealing credentials for Microsoft 365. Alternatively, exploiting unpatched, internet-facing servers (T1190 - Exploit Public-Facing Application) is also common.
Persistence & Privilege Escalation: Once inside, attackers often create new admin accounts or use tools like Mimikatz (S0002) to dump credentials (T1003 - OS Credential Dumping) and escalate privileges within Active Directory.
Discovery & Data Collection: Attackers would then perform discovery to locate servers and file shares containing patient data (PHI/EHR). They would then aggregate this data (T1074 - Data Staged) before exfiltration.
Exfiltration: Data is typically exfiltrated over common protocols like HTTPS to cloud storage providers to blend in with normal traffic (T1567.002 - Exfiltration Over Web Service: Exfiltration to Cloud Storage).

Impact Assessment
A data breach at a healthcare provider of Ochsner Health's size can have devastating consequences. The exposure of PHI can lead to identity theft, financial fraud, and targeted scams against vulnerable patients. The organization itself faces significant regulatory fines under HIPAA, potential class-action lawsuits, and severe reputational damage. The incident also underscores the systemic risk in the healthcare industry's heavy reliance on single-vendor technology stacks and the cascading impact when that infrastructure is compromised.

SBC Medical Group Reports Data Breach Affecting Over Two Million People

SBC Medical Group, a California-based medical services organization confirmed a data breach on November 16, 2026, after detecting anomalous activity on its Japanese subsidiary's systems. The company filed a report with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) detailing two separate security incidents that impacted its operations in Japan:unauthorized access to a website database managed by SBC Medical Group, Ltd.,administrator accounts on the third-party reservation platform Tribeau.Attackers used approximately 770,000 login attempts from overseas locations to breach the company's databases. The investigation found that customer passwords were stored without encryption. In the separate Tribeau incident, hackers compromised administrator credentials for 56 clinics to access patient booking details. The company isolated the affected servers and invalidated all clinic account passwords on the third-party platform to stop the breach.The exposed data includes:Full names, addresses, and phone numbersEmail addresses and unencrypted passwordsDates of birth and genderPatient card numbers and member IDsTreatment descriptions and reservation requestsEmployee bank account and pension informationWithholding tax certificates and dependent declarationsExpired credit card numbers for 14 individualsThe breach affected 1,624,000 individuals in the primary database and approximately 19,000 people through the Tribeau platform. Additionally, the attackers stole 20,000 employee records, including sensitive financial and tax data for 459 staff members. SBC Medical Group claims that clinical care systems and direct treatment histories were not stored in the compromised databases.SBC Medical Group notified Japan's Personal Information Protection Commission and is working with law enforcement. The company hired outside cybersecurity specialists for a forensic investigation. SBC Medical Group advises users to change their passwords and be careful of suspicious communications and phishing attempts.

CrowdStrike reportedly in talks to acquire cybersecurity provider Zscaler

by Maria Deutscher

CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. is reportedly in talks to buy Zscaler Inc., a publicly traded provider of cybersecurity software.
Sources told Bloomberg today that the acquisition could “come together soon.” However, they cautioned that it’s still possible the talks will fall through. 
Investors seem to be confident that the deal will materialize. Zscaler’s share price jumped more than 16% in after-hours trading, while CrowdStrike dropped about 4.8%. 
Software buyouts tend to value the acquired company at a premium to its last unaffected market capitalization. As a result, CrowdStrike is likely to pay more than the $32 billion Zscaler was worth at the end of today’s trading session. That means the deal could take CrowdStrike’s market capitalization above $250 billion.
CrowdStrike sells one of the world’s most popular cybersecurity platforms. Falcon can detect and block malicious activity across cloud instances, on-premises servers, employee devices and other assets. It also automates certain related tasks, such as finding sensitive records that are stored in an insecure manner.
Zscaler competes in a different part of the cybersecurity market. It sells software that protects the network connections through which a company’s employees access its business applications.
Enterprises historically used virtual private network, or VPN, tools for that task. Such programs tend to be quite slow. More significantly, they give employees access to the entire corporate network rather than to the specific applications they need for their work. That broad access can create cybersecurity risks.
Zscaler sells a zero-trust network access, or ZTNA, platform designed to replace legacy VPN software. It limits the number of applications that workers can access within the corporate network. If Zscaler detects risky activity, it asks the affected user to complete additional authentication steps.
The company’s ZTNA software doubles as an observability tool. Administrators can monitor employees’ connections for technical issues that may hinder productivity. A built-in artificial intelligence assistant, the ZDX Agent, generates troubleshooting advice.
Zscaler also competes in other product categories where CrowdStrike has a limited presence. Notably, it offers a tool that deploys bogus applications, user passwords and files in customer networks. Those simulated assets act as sensors. When an attempt is made to access one of them, Zscaler Deception notifies the customer that a cyberattack is underway.
The potential deal would mark CrowdStrike’s largest acquisition by a wide margin. The company’s biggest buyout to date is its $970 million purchase of startup SGNL Inc., which closed earlier this year. The deal bought CrowdStrike a platform that can automatically end users’ application sessions when it detects cybersecurity issues.

FCC to propose regulations for Cyber Trust Mark IoT labeling program

The commission hopes the program will encourage device manufacturers to prioritize cybersecurity.

Published Nov. 20, 2026

The seal for the Federal Communications Commission is seen in the agency’s headquarters on Feb. 18, 2026, in Washington, D.C. The FCC is considering sunsetting the E-rate program, a federal discount broadband program for schools and libraries.

Kevin Dietsch via Getty Images

The Federal Communications Commission on Monday will propose regulatory details of the U.S. Cyber Trust Mark, its internet of things cybersecurity labeling program. The system is designed to give purchasers of smart devices more information about the devices’ digital security features.
In a Federal Register notice scheduled for publication on Nov. 23, the commission said it was seeking comment on “the design and placement of the FCC IoT Label, display of product registry information, certification renewal, post-market surveillance, and procedures for complaints, noncompliant products, and program administrators that withdraw or whose authority is terminated.”

The Cyber Trust Mark program, which began during the Biden administration, is meant to stem the tide of cyberattacks exploiting vulnerabilities in IoT devices by encouraging manufacturers to develop more secure products. IoT products that pass tests administered by government-accredited labs will be eligible to display the Cyber Trust Mark label, which will contain a QR code pointing to product security details in a government registry.
The proposed rule, which will be open for public comment through Dec. 23, lists requirements for initial certification, renewals, eviction from the program and adjudication of complaints about misuse of the label.
Other provisions describe what the physical label should look like, how product security information should be displayed online (the digital records will resemble food nutrition labels) and how the companies administering the program should conduct “post-market surveillance” to ensure that IoT devices actually meet promised safety standards.
The FCC is also proposing a system of “ad-hoc surveillance” to investigate potentially systemic IoT device vulnerabilities after a major cyberattack that involves hacked devices. At the commission’s direction, the labeling program’s administrators would develop a testing plan, collect IoT devices from vendors, test them and report back to the FCC. In its proposed rule, the commission asked commenters to weigh in on how such testing should work, including whether program administrators should be able to initiate it without instruction from the FCC.

Program was a long time in the making
The Cyber Trust Mark program has been in development since 2023, but after gaining initial approval in the final year of the Biden administration, it hit a roadblock in January 2026 when the lead administrator withdrew over concerns about its ties to the Chinese government. In the months leading up to that withdrawal, some experts had questioned whether the FCC’s new Republican leadership remained committed to the program. But in April, the FCC signaled its renewed support for the labeling program when it picked a new organization to lead the effort.
Last month, FCC Chair Brendan Carr tapped his Republican colleague Olivia Trusty to oversee the program’s rollout in partnership with the commission’s homeland-security bureau, which will manage it.
“Our goal is a program that is practical for manufacturers, credible to consumers, and effective in encouraging better security across the marketplace,” Trusty said.

The Threat Disruption Center brings investigators and companies together to disrupt criminal networks targeting Americans

It aims to help warn victims sooner, interrupt payments, and take down scam infrastructure

If you’ve been scammed, report it promptly to the FBI’s IC3; don’t wait for the center

When someone realizes they have been scammed, the obvious question is: Can I get my money back?

A new US initiative aims to improve the chances of intervening before stolen money disappears—and, perhaps more importantly, before victims send more money.

The Threat Disruption Center will connect investigators with participating companies to help pause payments, freeze funds, take down malicious domains, and ban accounts scammers use to approach victims. TRM Labs is providing the investigative technology behind the effort.

TRM Labs is an existing blockchain intelligence company that helps financial institutions, crypto businesses, and government agencies detect and investigate crypto-related financial crime and fraud. It has been selected as the center’s primary private-sector partner.

The Threat Disruption Center sits within the Homeland Security Task Force’s National Coordination Center, which is co-led by the Department of Homeland Security and the Department of Justice. It will serve as a shared technology and collaboration resource for a task force that includes more than 30 federal agencies and over 440 state and local partners.

The reason

The practical aim is to help investigators sort through victim reports, connect related activity, and identify opportunities to intervene. TRM’s CEO told Bloomberg that the company is looking at how artificial intelligence (AI) can help triage reports in near real time and highlight cases where quick action could return funds to victims.

Scammers depend on legitimate services to reach people and move their money: social networks, website hosts, banks, payment providers, and cryptocurrency platforms. Those dependencies also create opportunities to interrupt them.

The center is intended to provide a standing channel through which investigators and participating companies can share intelligence in near real time. Depending on the circumstances, a company could then:

Pause a victim’s payment

Freeze stolen funds

Take down a malicious domain

Ban a social media account used to approach victims

The intended beneficiaries are anyone targeted by scams, cybercrime, and sextortion, not just people who own cryptocurrency. For consumers, the most valuable intervention may be the payment they never make.

Cryptocurrency investment scams often unfold over time. A scammer builds trust, introduces an apparently profitable investment opportunity, and encourages the victim to keep adding money. The FBI says some victims identified through its existing Operation Level Up initiative were preparing to sell their homes, liquidate retirement savings, or take out substantial loans. Reaching someone before that next transfer can prevent an already serious loss from becoming much worse.

What it’s not

Tracing money, freezing it, seizing it, and returning it to a victim are different stages. The announcements describe interventions intended to preserve funds while investigations and legal proceedings continue.

It should not be mistaken for a new public-facing recovery service, and it does not guarantee that victims will get their money back. The announced route for reporting a scam remains the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center, or IC3.

Do not wait for a new initiative to reach you. The FBI recommends:

Stop sending money immediately. Do not pay additional “taxes,” “verification charges,” or withdrawal fees demanded by a suspicious investment platform.

Report the scam promptly at ic3.gov. Rapid reporting can support recovery efforts and help investigators connect related complaints.

PHP2Shell aftershock: 18 more PHP flaws put enterprise web admins on alert

News

Nov 20, 20266 mins

PHP continues to root out flaws in its architecture, this week releasing fixes for a slew of additional security issues in the wake of PHP2Shell.

The patches address 18 vulnerabilities, including a critical request smuggling flaw that could allow unauthenticated attackers to remotely execute code on vulnerable servers. Other vulnerabilities affect PHP’s core engine, session handling, process manager, and Common Gateway Interface (CGI) protocol, which bridges web servers with external application programs.

The updates were released for all supported PHP versions, with PHP 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37, and 8.2.36 containing the fixes.

The disclosure comes as enterprises continue to grapple with the full impact of PHP2Shell, a pair of 9.2-severity-rated vulnerabilities disclosed in October. The flaws prompted the outright shutdown of some government websites, and, by some estimates, have borne the brunt of millions of exploit attempts.

“Enterprises should read this release as PHP2Shell’s aftershock: Smaller, but it shakes the same walls,” said Frank Dickson of Dickson Research.

Flaws enabling RCE, DoS, memory corruption

One of the most serious flaws disclosed this week, CVE-2026-129289, is rated a critical 9.2 on the Common Vulnerabilities Scoring System (CVSS). The request smuggling vulnerability impacts PHP-FPM, a background service that executes code for high-volume websites and apps.

If exploited, the flaw could allow unauthenticated actors to execute PHP code remotely on vulnerable servers that reuse connections to PHP-FPM under certain conditions. It impacts specific nginx, Apache, HAProxy, and LSAPI configurations that reuse backend connections to PHP-FPM.

When paired with a code execution bug, it can “carry an attacker from the web worker toward the whole server,” Dickson explained.

Several of the other patches also address vulnerabilities that could allow remote code execution (RCE). Still others address issues including information disclosure, memory corruption, denial-of-service (DoS) interruptions, potentially unsafe handling of HTTPS and FTPS URLs, and cross-site scripting.

While there may be heavy focus on the 9.2-rated CVE-2026-129289, the lesser flaws still matter, Dickson said. For instance, in one case, one capital letter turned off encryption; a URL written as HTTPS:// or FTPS:// with an uppercase S could send passwords, tokens, form data, and files in plaintext, even through a redirect, to anyone watching the network.

Not quite PHP2Shell level, but still high priority

An attacker who exploits a PHP code-execution flaw gains access to whatever the PHP worker can touch, “which is just about everything,” Dickson said. Successful exploitation executes code with the privileges of the PHP worker, which holds the database password, API keys, cloud credentials, and session data.

For example, he described what he called an “ugly” attack path:

The threat actor gets in through the web application.

Reads the configuration file;

Dumps the customer database;

Plants a web shell to come back later.

He pointed out that PHP warned that PHP2Shell puts every installation serving web requests at risk, with no login required. “This release returns to the same neighborhood: session upload progress, fatal error backtraces, and how PHP behaves when it runs out of memory,” he said.

Fritz Jean-Louis, principal cybersecurity advisor at Infotech, agreed that this is a high-priority patching event, if not a PHP2Shell-level emergency. Although several of the critical vulnerabilities require specific configurations or uncommon deployment scenarios, “they still affect one of the most widely deployed web runtimes in the world,” he noted.

Researchers planted 2 million digital tripwires in requests sent through a sprawling network of AI services to find out what happened to sensitive information entrusted to them. What they discovered was an ecosystem that leaked highly sensitive data like a sieve.
The exposure was found through an ingenious experiment designed to test if sensitive information can leak through the vast chain of widely used AI services and how that information is exploited when it does. Many of today’s AI apps use services such as OpenRouter or Vercel that act as brokers. These “AI routers,” sometimes also known as “AI gateways,” receive large numbers of prompts sent from AI app end users and route them to an available inference engine based on criteria such as the one charging the lowest price or being best suited for the given task. Instead of using Anthropic, OpenAI, or another big provider, the developer hires an AI router to find the most suitable model.
Update, Nov 21: Posts on both Hacker News and X report that OpenRouter has sent customers an email notifying them that some of their prompts may have been read. OpenRouter cited the research and said that it received a report that the potential exposure involved prompts sent to MiniMax, a China-based model provider. OpenRouter said the researchers’ planted URLs were accessed whether the prompts were sent to MiniMax directly or through three other resellers: AtlasCloud, Novita, and StreamLake. OpenRouter has removed a “Zero Data Retention” label from MiniMax-model endpoints. Hat tip: Sulat.com.
Security breaches, prompt theft, and privacy violations
To test for potential leakage, researcher HD Moore assembled a collection of Amazon Web Services access keys, functioning credentials tied to empty AWS accounts, passwords for services such as SSH, and unique URLs, DNS names, and private git repository references. None of the secrets had ever been used before, and he controlled the infrastructure that received any requests using the credentials. He then seeded each secret into exactly one prompt sent to a single provider. In the event any of the secrets were leaked, these “canaries”—so called because they resemble the role of that bird when taken into coal mines—would allow Moore to identify each link in the chain that was responsible.

The findings are striking. They included:

Evidence that at least three AI providers were compromised by attackers who used their access to siphon prompts they received
Multiple resellers in the inference marketplace that logged the prompts and somehow passed them along to people who used the credentials
Multiple cases of AI providers not following end-user privacy settings embedded into flags specifying terms such as Zero Data Retention (ZDR) or “no data collection”

“We sent nearly two million AI prompts containing unique, trackable secrets to AI providers, then watched where those secrets surfaced,” Moore, the chief research officer of security firm Dragos, wrote Thursday. “What we found revealed security breaches, prompt theft, and widespread failures to protect customer data.”
Although prompts are encrypted in transit, they are decrypted at each hop inside the large inference reseller network. The prompt is first sent to an AI router, which reads the plaintext in it to determine the most suitable inference providers to handle the request. Often, the prompt is then sent to a pool of available models, which sometimes run inside different hosting providers. Prompts can also pass from one AI router (such as Vercel) to another one (e.g., OpenRouter). Each one of these players is likely to log the prompt and store it for as long as its policies call for (if not indefinitely).
